audit_notes: All nine parameters are positive and lie inside their stated bounds; values are consistent with low-density carbon/ceramic foam TPS (PICA-class density 280 kg/m3, cp 1200 J/kg/K, k_s 0.05 W/m/K). No adjustment required. Non-linearity check: k(T) = k_s + 4*sigma*d*T^3 gives k(300 K) = 0.0512 W/m/K and k(2000 K) = 0.413 W/m/K, a factor ~8 increase, so the problem is strongly non-linear as requested. Thermal load: radiative-equilibrium surface temperature at the 0.5 MW/m2 peak is (q/(eps*sigma))^0.25 = 1795 K; the actual peak will be somewhat lower because part of the flux is conducted/stored. This is within the service limit of SiC-coated carbon foam (~1900-2000 K in oxidising flow) but leaves a modest margin, so peak_heat_flux values near the 2 MW/m2 upper bound (T_eq ~ 2540 K) would exceed the material limit and should be treated as infeasible in any sweep. Mechanical: no significant structural load in the 1D thermal model; a 280 kg/m3 foam has crush strength of order 1-5 MPa, well above re-entry stagnation pressures (~10-50 kPa). Bondline: typical adhesive/structure limit ~520 K (250 C); cold-side Fourier number Fo = alpha*t_pulse/L^2 ~ 0.02 (0.12 at 1800 K conductivity) indicates the thermal wave penetrates roughly 0.5-1 cm of the 3 cm during the pulse, so the bondline should stay cool during the pulse itself. Caveats: (1) the time domain in the formulation is one pulse duration only, so post-pulse soak-back into the bondline is not captured; (2) the fourth 'boundary condition' T(x,1) is not a condition - the problem is an initial-boundary-value problem (parabolic in t) and must be marched in time, not solved as a 2D elliptic BVP. Simulation coefficient returned is the time-scaling coefficient pulse_duration/(rho*cp*L^2) = 0.397 m*K/W that multiplies k(T) in the normalised PDE. Solver: transient, strongly non-linear with a non-linear (radiative, T^4) Robin boundary -> dynamic_script (method of lines with implicit stiff integrator). Objective: minimise the peak bondline temperature rise; reported as percent reduction relative to an otherwise identical coarse-pore (1 mm, pumice-like) reference foam, which isolates the benefit of the cork-like small-pore design.
